headline: Pakistan Creates 400-km Dolphin Sanctuary as River Recovery Gains Momentum
meta_description: Pakistan has established a new protected corridor for the endangered Indus River dolphin, connecting reserves across two provinces as the species rebounds from…
summary_short: Pakistan's new Punjnad sanctuary joins an existing reserve to form a continuous 400-kilometer protected corridor for the critically endangered Indus River dolphin, local…
body:
In June 2026, Pakistan created the Punjnad Indus River Dolphin Sanctuary in Punjab, establishing nearly 200 kilometers of legally protected habitat for one of the world's rarest freshwater dolphins. This new reserve connects seamlessly with an existing protected area in Sindh province, forming a continuous 400-kilometer corridor—a lifeline for a species that has endured centuries of habitat loss and near-extinction. The timing is crucial: a 2025 study published in Endangered Species Research documented that the Indus River dolphin population has rebounded to approximately 1,987 individuals, representing a 19.4% increase between 2011 and 2017. This recovery offers genuine hope for the bhulan, the local name for this evolutionary marvel that has navigated the river on its side using echolocation for millions of years.

Yet the dolphins remain in precarious circumstances. Nearly 99% of the surviving population is confined to a 690-kilometer stretch between the Chashma barrage in Punjab and the Sukkur barrage in Sindh. Gillnet entanglement accounts for 52% of documented dolphin deaths between 2008 and 2023, a threat compounded by commercial fishing contracts that prioritize profit over wildlife protection. The species has already lost approximately 80% of its historical range, and fewer than 1,000 individuals existed as recently as 2001.

Conservationists emphasize that long-term survival depends on cross-provincial coordination and fundamental changes to how the river operates. Modifying barrage operations, regulating commercial fishing practices, and supporting community-led sustainable fishing are essential steps. Pakistan now bears unique global responsibility: the overwhelming majority of the species exists only within its borders, with only a small remnant population remaining in India's Beas River. The new sanctuary represents recognition of this obligation—and a commitment to ensuring that the Queen of the Indus River survives for generations to come.
quick_facts: Pakistan created Punjnad Sanctuary protecting 200 km of river in June 2026
New reserve connects with Sindh's existing reserve to form 400 km corridor
Indus River dolphin population rebounded to 1,987 individuals by 2025
Nearly 99% of dolphins live in 690 km stretch between two barrages
Gillnet entanglement caused 52% of dolphin deaths between 2008–2023
